2.1.crux: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope; the main groups are bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses.

cards.title: Tiny living things
say: Microorganisms (microbes) are so small that we need a microscope to see them.
Some, like bread mould, can be seen with a magnifying glass when they grow in large groups.

cards.title: Meet the five groups
say: Bacteria, fungi, protozoa and algae are the four main groups.
Viruses are different: they can only multiply inside the cells of another living thing.

cards.title: What makes viruses special

cols.head: Other microbes
cells: Live and grow on their own

cols.head: Viruses
cells: Multiply only inside another organism's cells
Cause cold, flu, polio, chicken pox

say: A virus outside a living cell cannot reproduce.
Inside a host cell, it makes many copies of itself.
cards.remember: Viruses multiply only inside the cells of a host.

crux_points: Microorganisms are too small to see without a microscope.
The main groups are bacteria, fungi, protozoa and algae.
Viruses multiply only inside the cells of other living things.

quiz.why: This is a virus: the smallest microbe, which reproduces only inside host cells.

quiz.q: Bread mould belongs to which group?
quiz.why: Moulds that grow on bread are fungi.

2.2.crux: Microbes live almost everywhere: in air, water, soil, ice, hot springs and inside the bodies of plants and animals.

cards.title: Microbes are everywhere
say: Microbes can survive in very cold and very hot places.
They also live inside animals, including humans.

cards.title: One cell or many
say: Some microbes are just one cell. Others are made of many cells.
Some live alone; others grow together in colonies.

cards.title: Where can you find them today?
say: Microbes are around us all the time.
Most are harmless, and many are useful.
cards.think: Why do we wash our hands before eating?

crux_points: Microbes live in air, water, soil and inside living things.
They survive even in ice and hot springs.
They can be single-celled or many-celled, alone or in colonies.

quiz.q: Can microbes live in hot springs?
quiz.why: Some microbes survive in very hot places like hot springs.
Bread mould is a fungus made of many cells.

2.3.crux: Many microbes are our friends: they make curd and bread, give us medicines and vaccines, enrich the soil and clean up waste.

cards.title: Microbes in the kitchen

items.name: Curd
items.eg: Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk into curd

say: A little curd added to warm milk makes the whole bowl into curd.
Lactobacillus bacteria in the curd multiply and do the work.

cards.title: How yeast makes dough rise

steps.text: Yeast is added to dough with a little sugar
Yeast grows and gives off carbon dioxide gas
Gas bubbles fill the dough, so it becomes soft and spongy

say: Yeast changes sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. This is called fermentation.
Louis Pasteur discovered fermentation in 1857.
cards.remember: Fermentation: yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

cards.title: Medicines from microbes

cols.head: Vaccine
cells: Trains the body to fight a disease in future

say: Antibiotics are made from bacteria and fungi.
Antibiotics do NOT work against colds and flu, because these are caused by viruses.

cards.title: Helpers for the planet

items.sub: Some bacteria and blue-green algae fix nitrogen
Decompose dead plants and animals into manure

say: Microbes break down dead plants, animals and kitchen waste into simple substances.
Plants can use these substances again.

crux_points: Lactobacillus makes curd; yeast makes bread rise and makes alcohol by fermentation.
Antibiotics and vaccines come from or use microbes.
Microbes enrich the soil and clean the environment by decomposing waste.

quiz.q: Which microbe turns milk into curd?
quiz.why: Lactobacillus bacteria multiply in milk and turn it into curd.

quiz.q: Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added?
quiz.why: Yeast breathes out carbon dioxide; its bubbles make the dough rise.

quiz.q: Should you take antibiotics for a common cold?
options: No, colds are caused by viruses
quiz.why: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses like the cold virus.

2.4.crux: Some microbes cause diseases in people, animals and plants, and some spoil food; disease-causing microbes are called pathogens.

cards.title: How germs spread

items.sub: Sneezes and coughs: TB, measles, chicken pox
Touching a sick person or their things

say: Diseases that spread from one person to another are called communicable diseases.

cards.title: Carriers
say: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water.
Keep surroundings clean and don't let water collect.
cards.remember: No stagnant water = fewer mosquitoes = less malaria and dengue.

cards.title: Diseases in humans
say: Many of these diseases can be prevented by vaccines and hygiene.

cards.title: In animals and plants

pic.root: Microbes harm animals and crops too

say: Crop diseases lower the harvest and can cause big losses to farmers.

cards.title: Food poisoning

steps.text: Food is left out or kept badly
Microbes grow on it and make poisonous substances
Eating it makes a person very ill

say: Spoiled food can smell bad, taste sour or show fungus.
That is why food must be preserved properly.

crux_points: Pathogens are microbes that cause disease.
Germs spread through air, water, food, contact and carriers like flies and mosquitoes.
Microbes also cause diseases in animals and plants and spoil food.

quiz.q: Which insect carries the malaria parasite?
quiz.why: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the protozoan that causes malaria.

quiz.q: Cholera and typhoid usually spread through…
quiz.why: These bacteria spread through contaminated water and food.

2.5.crux: We preserve food by stopping microbes from growing, using salt, sugar, oil and vinegar, heating, cold, pasteurisation and airtight packs.

cards.title: Ways to keep food fresh

items.name: Salt
items.eg: Fish, meat, amla, raw mango, tamarind

items.name: Chemicals
items.eg: Sodium benzoate in jams and squashes

say: Salt and sugar pull water out of food, and microbes can't grow without water.
Oil and vinegar stop bacteria from living in pickles.

cards.title: Pasteurised milk

steps.text: Milk is heated to about 70°C for 15 to 30 seconds
It is packed and stored cold

say: Heating kills the microbes; sudden cooling stops new ones growing.
Louis Pasteur discovered this method, so it is called pasteurisation.
cards.remember: Pasteurised milk can be drunk without boiling.

cards.title: Packing keeps germs out
say: Airtight packs stop microbes from reaching the food.

crux_points: Preservation stops microbes from growing on food.
Salt, sugar, oil, vinegar and chemicals are common preservatives.
Heating, cold, pasteurisation and airtight packing also keep food safe.

options: Heated to about 70°C, then suddenly chilled
quiz.why: Pasteurisation heats milk briefly to kill microbes, then cools it quickly.

quiz.q: Why does sugar keep jam from spoiling?
options: It removes the water microbes need
quiz.why: Sugar draws out moisture, so bacteria can't grow.

2.6.crux: Plants need nitrogen but can't take it from the air; bacteria like Rhizobium in root nodules and blue-green algae fix it into the soil.

cards.title: Nitrogen: everywhere but locked away
say: Air is about 78% nitrogen.
Plants and animals need nitrogen to make proteins, but they can't use nitrogen gas directly from the air.

cards.title: Bacteria in root nodules

labels.name: Root nodule
labels.note: A small lump on the root

say: Rhizobium bacteria live inside small lumps (nodules) on the roots of pea and bean plants.
They take nitrogen from the air and turn it into compounds the plant can use.
cards.remember: Rhizobium + legume roots = nitrogen fixed in the soil.

cards.title: Ways nitrogen gets fixed
say: Changing nitrogen gas into usable compounds is called nitrogen fixation.
This is why farmers grow legumes: they make the soil richer.

crux_points: Air is mostly nitrogen, but plants can't use it directly.
Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules fix nitrogen into the soil.
Blue-green algae and lightning also fix nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is marked '?' on the roots?
quiz.why: These small lumps are root nodules, where Rhizobium bacteria live.

quiz.q: Which bacterium fixes nitrogen in the roots of legumes?
quiz.why: Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants.

2.7.crux: Nitrogen keeps moving in a loop: from air into soil, into plants and animals, and back to the air when bacteria break down their remains.

cards.title: Why living things need nitrogen

items.sub: The green pigment plants use to make food

say: Nitrogen is an essential part of proteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acids and vitamins.
So every plant and animal needs a steady supply of it.

cards.title: The nitrogen cycle

steps.text: The air has a huge store of nitrogen gas.
Bacteria, blue-green algae and lightning turn it into compounds in the soil.
Plants take in these compounds through their roots to make proteins.
Animals get nitrogen by eating plants.
When plants and animals die, bacteria and fungi break them down into compounds in the soil.
Some bacteria change these compounds back into nitrogen gas.

say: Because nitrogen keeps going round, the amount in the air stays almost the same.
cards.remember: Air → soil → plants → animals → decay → air.

cards.title: Decomposers close the loop

steps.text: Nitrogen compounds return to the soil for new plants

say: Without decomposers, nitrogen would stay locked in dead bodies.

crux_points: Nitrogen moves between air, soil and living things in a cycle.
Fixation puts nitrogen into soil; plants take it up and animals eat plants.
Decomposers and some bacteria return nitrogen to the soil and air.

options: By eating plants or other animals
quiz.why: Animals can't use nitrogen gas; they get it from the proteins in their food.

quiz.q: Who returns nitrogen from dead plants and animals to the soil?
quiz.why: Decomposers break down dead remains into nitrogen compounds in the soil.
